[evals] Add EconEvals synthetic DWA and occupation benchmarks (#11614)

Add the [EconEvals](https://econevals.com/)
([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19375)) synthetic DWA and occupation
benchmarks as curated chat evals. Each item is a workplace request; a
judge compares the candidate's answer with a released baseline answer
using EconEvals' Arena-Hard prompt, once in each order. A decisive
verdict counts as three games and a tie as half a win, so the weighted
mean `win_rate` is 0.5 at parity with the baseline. Questions, baseline
answers and category tables are pinned to a revision of
`EconEvals/EconEvalsIntermediate`. verifyit gains a `pairwise` judge
rubric for the two-order comparison.

| Suite | Baseline | Items (DWA / occupation) |
|---|---|---|
| `econevals` | o3-mini (the paper's) | 2,351 / 2,426 |
| `econevals-o3` | o3 | 2,351 / 2,426 |
| `econevals-sampled` | o3-mini | 240 / 258 |
| `econevals-sampled-o3` | o3 | 240 / 258 |

Strong models beat o3-mini on most items, so the `-o3` suites keep
headroom. The sampled suites keep a fixed six questions per category for
development runs: a full run took 6–12 hours of generation, and Muse
Glimmer 30B finished `econevals-sampled-o3` in about an hour on 2 H100s.
The judge is Together's `openai/gpt-oss-120b`; the paper used
gpt-4.1-mini, so scores are not directly comparable with it. The sampled
Glimmer run cost an estimated $1–2 in judge calls.

| Model | Suite | DWA | Occupation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | `econevals` | 0.106 | 0.098 |
| Qwen3-8B | `econevals-sampled` | 0.098 | 0.105 |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | `econevals-sampled-o3` | 0.370 ± 0.055 | 0.443 ±
0.055 |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | `econevals-sampled-o3` | 0.687 ± 0.053 | 0.635 ±
0.051 |
| Snowball v0.1 | `econevals-sampled-o3` | 0.165 ± 0.038 | 0.170 ± 0.039
|

The judge often prefers whichever answer it reads first. On 17%
(Qwen3-8B vs o3-mini) to 40% (Glimmer vs o3) of items the two orders
disagree, and each such item scores 0.5; the paper's released
gpt-4.1-mini judgments split on 48% of gpt-4.1 vs o3-mini items. In a
blinded review of 40 Glimmer vs o3 items by two Claude reviewers (kappa
0.68), the judge contradicted the reviewers' consensus on 24% of the
items it decided the same way in both orders (95% CI 7–44%), and its
population-weighted win rate for Glimmer was 0.38 against the reviewers'
0.47. The suites therefore separate models that are far apart, but score
differences under about 0.1 are noise. The judge and the o3 baseline are
both OpenAI models, so self-preference may contribute to the judge's gap
with the reviewers. A stronger, non-OpenAI judge is follow-up work.

The judge also favors longer answers. On `econevals-sampled-o3`, each
doubling of the candidate's length relative to o3's adds about 0.22 to
an item's score. Nemotron 3.5 Super's answers are longer than o3's on
78% of items (median 1,208 words against o3's 922), Glimmer's on 38%. On
the 170 questions where Nemotron and Glimmer answers are of similar
length, Nemotron scores 0.015 higher; on the 302 where Nemotron's is
clearly longer, 0.33 higher. At equal length the gap between them
shrinks from 0.21 to about 0.09, while Snowball v0.1 trails at every
length. Longer answers may also be more complete, so this does not show
how much of the effect is bias. A length-controlled score, like
Arena-Hard's style control, is follow-up work.

Baseline answers are OpenAI outputs and the recipes are eval-only; they
must not enter training data. The real-query DWA benchmark is not
included: its prompts point into LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat and must be
rebuilt from those corpora. The EconEvals data and code repositories
declare no license; Marin downloads the pinned files at run time and
does not redistribute them. The judge prompts derive from
Arena-Hard-Auto (Apache-2.0).

[iris] Write controller job, config and attempt rows to Finelog (#11037)

tl;dr human tokens: after this change, when iris operations update the
jobs, job_config, tasks and task_attempts tables of controller_db, the
rows changed are now to mirrored (- some fields) to finelog. The changed
rows are captured in a pre-commit hook (of the controller DB
transaction), and the write to finelog happens if the commit goes
through.

🤖 
This replaces #10987, which was opened from a fork. Its review threads,
including the Codex findings and their fixes, are there. The branch and
commits are the same, now pushed to this repository so that a follow-up
can stack on it.

Copy the controller DB's `jobs`, `job_config`, `tasks` and
`task_attempts` rows to four Finelog namespaces:
`iris.controller_db__jobs`, `iris.controller_db__job_config`,
`iris.controller_db__tasks` and `iris.controller_db__task_attempts`. The
controller DB deletes terminal jobs after 7 days, and the
attempt-to-node mapping exists only there, so utilization queries could
not join requests and placement with node telemetry beyond that window.
The `iris.controller_db__` prefix separates these copies from Iris's
measurement and event namespaces, such as `iris.task` and
`iris.task_state`.

The rows carry a chosen set of columns, plus the job key. A column is
copied when the controller or a fixed vocabulary writes its value: ids,
keys, states, enums, times, counts, resource numbers, policies and
placement. Rows are kept forever, so text the user wrote is left out
rather than redacted, with two exceptions: the free-text error columns,
redacted, and the launch's git identity, read from the environment.

- From `job_config`, these are not copied: the environment (env vars and
secrets) apart from the git identity below, `entrypoint_json`,
`submit_argv_json`, `bundle_id`, `ports_json`, `egress_allow_json`, and
the duplicate `name`. From `tasks`, the scheduler's queue order
(`priority_neg_depth`, `priority_insertion`) and
`current_worker_address`, which `iris.worker` already records per
worker, are not copied either: Finelog columns can be added later but
never dropped. Every other column of `jobs`, `tasks` and `task_attempts`
is copied.
- The free-text `error` columns and `tasks.status_message` stay
readable, with token-like strings redacted.
- The DB's `cluster` (local, or the peer a job was handed to) is stored
as `placement`, because `cluster` here names the writing controller.
- `job_config` also gets `accelerator_kind`, `accelerator_type` and
`accelerators_per_task`, flattened from the device request.
- `job_config` also gets four fields of the job's `MARIN_PROVENANCE`
(the launch's git provenance): `provenance_base_commit`,
`provenance_tree_hash`, `provenance_dirty` and `provenance_branch`, the
branch with token-like strings redacted. The rest of that variable is
not copied: its command line and remote URL are user text that can hold
a credential, and its user and launch time are already on the job rows.
`rigging.provenance.Provenance.from_json` now checks the payload's shape
and raises `ValueError` on any malformed value; such a value leaves the
four columns NULL and the job's rows are still written.

A test lists every column of the four controller DB tables as copied or
excluded, and fails on any column it doesn't list. A controller schema
change therefore gets a one-line decision instead of silently going
uncopied. A dropped DB column that was copied keeps its Finelog field,
which reads NULL from then on.

`lib/iris/docs/observability-rows.md` gives the rule, the excluded
columns, the keys, the `cluster` values and example joins.

A write path that changes a job, task or attempt marks its id. A new
pre-commit hook on `Tx` reads the marked rows in batched queries just
before `COMMIT`, and the rows are written after commit through the same
non-blocking path as `iris.task_event`. The tables are append-only: an
entity's current state is its newest row by `(ts, seq)`. A job is keyed
by `(cluster, root_job_id, root_submitted_at_ms, job_id,
submitted_at_ms)`, because job ids are reused and a live parent can
resubmit a finished child under the same name; an attempt is keyed by
`attempt_uid`. A failed worker's attempts keep their `worker_id`:
`remove_worker` records it before clearing the column. `jobs` has a
nullable `tags` column for submit-time job tags. History is kept in the
archive; the storage policies bound only the hub's local copy.

A `tasks` row is written at submit and when the task's state, current
attempt, current worker, error or exit code changes. A change to any
other column alone writes no row, because Kubernetes rewrites the
pending reason (`status_message`) on every reconcile. The reconcile path
decides this from its in-memory snapshot, with no extra reads.

In tests, `make_controller_state` and the journey worlds check after
every committed transaction that each locally owned job, task or attempt
whose columns changed has a row written by that transaction. A new write
path that forgets to mark its rows then fails the controller tests
instead of silently dropping rows.

Only the controller that executes a job writes its rows. A job that the
`marin` controller hands off to a CoreWeave peer is written by that
peer, so each job has one writer and one key, and handed-off jobs appear
only after the CoreWeave controllers run this change. cw-us-west-04a is
a CI cluster, not forwarded to the hub.

`cluster` is the writing controller's cluster config name on every row,
on its own store and on the hub. A regional Finelog forwards the rows
named for its own `forwarding.cluster` (#11176), and a test checks that
each cluster config sets that to the cluster's name.
`ControllerConfig.cluster_id` is now required. A CoreWeave Finelog must
run #11176 before its controller runs this change, because an older
forwarder skips named rows.

Finelog writes never block the controller. A failed snapshot or enqueue
is logged (`observability rows: snapshot failed` or `observability rows:
write failed`) and drops that transaction's rows; the controller's
transaction still commits and its other post-commit hooks still run.

Write-path cost from `benchmark_controller.py reconcile --num-tasks 5000
--tasks-per-worker 64 --payload-bytes 102400` on a MacBook, two runs
each alternated with main (merge base f6c200af77). Mean ms; runs agree
within about 2%:

| Phase | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| Setup: submit and assign 5,000 tasks | 763 | 963 |
| Dispatch tick, 5,000 attempts to RUNNING | 616 | 775 |
| · apply | 319 | 460 |
| · snapshot | 17 | 44 |
| Steady tick, no state change | 263 | 293 |
| · apply | 221 | 250 |

- **Dispatch tick:** the extra cost is in **apply** (+141 ms), which is
where the rows are read, in the pre-commit hook. The move to RUNNING
writes about 10,000 rows (one task and one attempt row per attempt, plus
the job). They are read in batched `IN` queries (400 ids each), not one
query per entity. A profile shows the cost spread over decoding those
rows, building the row objects and the client's size estimate, roughly
30 µs per row; there is no single hotspot to remove while keeping every
column.
- **"snapshot"** is the controller's own read snapshot before the tick,
not the row reads. Its +27 ms is not isolated, like the steady tick's
difference below.
- **Steady tick:** writes no job rows; a test checks that a repeated
RUNNING report on a running job adds none. A worker observation that
changes nothing on the attempt row, such as a status-message refresh,
writes no attempt row either; a test checks that too. The remaining
difference is probably the in-process Finelog server and the client's
flush thread, which only the branch's benchmark starts. It has not been
isolated.
- **Setup** also includes starting that Finelog server, so it overstates
the cost of submit and assign.

`main`'s benchmark script fails at the merge base (`termination_grace
must be resolved before persistence`), so the main runs used main's
script plus this branch's 3-line `termination_grace` fix.

**Watching the cost in production:** the controller emits one
`iris_observability_rows_transaction` event to `telemetry_v1.iris` for
each transaction that copies rows, with its rows per table and its
snapshot and enqueue times (both under the write lock), so a burst's
cost can be read against its row count. Counts and durations only.
Write-lock hold and wait time go out once a minute as
`iris_controller_write_lock_held_seconds` and
`iris_controller_write_lock_wait_seconds`. Everything is emitted after
the lock is released. A transaction whose rows take over 100 ms is also
logged. Setting `finelog.controller_rows: false` in the cluster config
turns the copy off when the controller restarts; the lock-time counters
keep flowing for comparison. `lib/iris/docs/observability-rows.md` has
the queries and the switch.

`iris.task_event`'s table is still passed to `Tx` on its own, and its
post-commit write in `reconcile/commit.py` can still raise into the
controller the same way. Guarding that write is a separate follow-up.

Follow-up: `LogStack` and `ObservabilityRowTables` both hold the four
row tables, and the tables are copied across one by one. Merging them
needs a type without `cluster`, because the cluster is known only after
`LogStack` is built. It is left for a later change.

[rl] Run Mochi and mixed-task Snowball from presets (#11728)

Run Mochi and mixed-task Snowball through the shared RL launcher. `--sft PRESET` trains or reuses an SFT export and initializes RL with its weights and tokenizer. `--resume NAME@VERSION` restores a committed native checkpoint and its starting model from a stopped run.

Mochi defaults to evaluating live weights and using three-day temporary output. Native saves and Hugging Face exports are available on request. The plan reports the selected output root. Ungated runs can set checkpoint retention, save cadence and export policy. The final receipt records the result before pruning, and a separate `--recover-best` command can recover the selected policy from a stopped run. Megatron exports range-backed checkpoints one Safetensors shard at a time.

The mixed presets take an explicit task selection. `snowball-100k-agentic@2026.11.19.2` contains 100,000 one-turn examples and 5,608 SWE tasks after EvalLite exclusion. Selection pins the released Parquet and graded admission evidence by digest. The agentic presets collect installed-agent attempts when RL commits. A separate skip command publishes exact-revision exclusions from repeated setup or verifier failures. Publishing a selection requires admission evidence from an existing probe.

The short Snowball pipeline completed five SFT steps, two one-turn RL updates and two 100-task EvalLite evaluations. Its export tokenizer reproduced a 4,095-token rollout prompt. [Short pipeline](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-snowball-rl-train-long-58b7969303-in-fbde17c5-2026.11.20.4-coordinator-82fa4b1c)

Both attempts of the 100-update `train-long` preset ran out of CUDA memory during the 24th optimizer update of their process. [evals] Add the LEXam multiple-choice benchmarks in English and German (#11778)

Add two chat benchmarks of multiple-choice questions from Swiss law
school exams: `lexam-mcq-4-en` with 619 English questions and
`lexam-mcq-4-de` with 1,036 German questions. Together they are the
four-choice test split of
[LEXam](https://huggingface.co/datasets/LEXam-Benchmark/LEXam)
([arXiv:2505.12864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12864)), pinned at
`31e57ae395f92ed7284a4c28d278c55da892b898`. They are separate so English
scores stay comparable while German tracks multilingual performance.
Each question lists three to five legal statements, and the four choices
are subsets of them. The prompt is the authors' `MCQ_PROMPT["letters"]`
from
[`litellm_eval.py`](https://github.com/LEXam-Benchmark/LEXam/blob/64f2e548a4a84b6154be3498dd5fed8966990bca/litellm_eval.py)
at `64f2e548`, which is in English for both languages. A new `lexam_mcq`
scorer takes the last `###X###` marker in the final answer and scores a
response without one as wrong, as the authors' `evaluation.py` does.
LEXam data is CC-BY-4.0, and its reference code (prompt and extraction)
is Apache-2.0. Neither benchmark is added to a suite.

The benchmarks add legal reasoning to the curated catalog. Statements
test concrete rules from Swiss statutes and case law. The questions ask
the model to reason step by step before giving the marked answer.

Each model keeps its served sampling defaults and token budget. The
reference caps output at 4,096 tokens, or 8,192 for models it treats as
reasoning models. The compiled prompts for all 1,655 questions match the
authors' rendering byte for byte. The scores below come from full-split
runs with the same prompts and scorer, split by language.

| Model | Hardware | English ± SE | German ± SE | No `###X###` marker
(en / de) | Stopped at context window (en / de) | Median output tokens
(en / de) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | H100x4 | 86.43 ± 1.38 | 52.80 ± 1.55 | 1 / 52 | 1
/ 52 | 11.7k / 28.9k |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | H100x2 | 74.96 ± 1.74 | 45.37 ± 1.55 | 53 / 129 | 0
/ 0 | 3.3k / 5.9k |
| Snowball v0.1 | H100x8 | 69.79 ± 1.85 | 42.47 ± 1.54 | 0 / 4 | 0 / 0 |
1.9k / 3.8k |
| Qwen3-32B | H100x2 | 63.33 ± 1.94 | 46.91 ± 1.55 | 13 / 6 | 0 / 0 |
1.8k / 2.9k |

German is much harder for every model, and the ranking changes:
Qwen3-32B moves from last in English to second in German. Nemotron's
German answers run long: 52 reach the context window, and 49 of those
end without an answer.

The paper reports Qwen3-32B only on the full German and English split:
45.30 ± 1.23. Our full-split run scores 53.05 ± 1.23, a gap of 4.5
combined standard errors. Rescoring our run as if output stopped at
4,096 tokens gives 43.1, within 1.2 standard errors of the paper. At
8,192 tokens it gives 53.0. The 4,096-token default in the authors'
lighteval runner explains the gap; a capped rerun has not been done.

Missing markers lower Glimmer's score more than the others'. Of its 53
English answers without a marker, most write `Correct Answer: X` without
the hashes. Also accepting that form would raise Glimmer by about 5
points in English and 4.4 in German, and the other models by at most
1.3. The English ranking does not change; in German, Glimmer would move
above Qwen3-32B. The strict rule is kept so scores stay comparable with
the paper.

Reading 38 graded English Glimmer answers found no grading errors. Where
Glimmer was wrong, the answer key held up, for example on the 0.4 mg/L
breath-alcohol threshold and on partnerships suing in their own name
under Art. 562 OR. A few percent of questions refer to context from the
original exam that the dataset omits. The English questions come from
four courses, and 544 of the 619 (88%) come from one 2019 Swiss Law
exam. German answers were not read.

Measured costs are for the full 1,655-question runs, which cover both
benchmarks, at the CoreWeave list price of $6.155 per GPU-hour.
Snowball's and Nemotron's inference workers were preempted. For those
two the range runs from the last attempt alone to the evaluation's full
wall time. English estimates scale each run's eval time by the English
share of its output tokens (23–30%), plus about 5 minutes of startup;
German accounts for the rest.

| Model | Full-split eval time | Full-split cost | English estimate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | 6.8 h | $118–168 | $30–41 |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | 49 min | $10.63 | $4 |
| Snowball v0.1 | 33 min | $19–27 | $6–12 |
| Qwen3-32B | 37 min | $8.24 | $3 |

Run records are under
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/lexam-mcq4-full-{glimmer,nemotron-super,snowball,qwen3-32b}-20261119-lexam-mcq-4-*`
([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fevals%2F)).
The open-question half of LEXam, graded by an LLM judge on a 0–1 scale,
is not included.

[levanter] Lock multi-process checkpoint commits on NFS with lock files (#10969)

Multi-node checkpoints saved to a shared NFS directory fail
intermittently; this makes TensorStore guard those saves with lock
files, which the NFS server enforces, so every save commits.

Levanter saves a checkpoint as one OCDBT store (TensorStore's
single-database format), and every process commits its writes to that
store's manifest file. TensorStore's local-file driver guards each
commit with advisory OS locks by default. Those locks do not exclude
writers on different NFS clients, so two nodes' commits race and one
fails with `Failed to rename ... manifest.ocdbt.__lock to ...
manifest.ocdbt: No such file or directory`. Training the June model on
two MI355X nodes with checkpoints on a shared NFS `/work`, the 7th of 7
saves failed at a 2 s save interval and 1 of 3 at a 10 s interval. GCS
and S3 checkpoints are unaffected because object stores arbitrate
commits with conditional writes.

`TensorStoreWriteConfig.file_io_locking` now selects the file driver's
locking mode. Left unset, it picks `lockfile` for multi-process saves to
local paths and keeps TensorStore's default for single-process and
object-store saves. A lock file is created exclusively, which the NFS
server enforces, so only one process commits the manifest at a time.

A lock file also outlives a process killed mid-commit, and TensorStore
then waits on it until its 60 s acquire timeout and fails. Levanter
reuses `step-N` directories, so without cleanup a run resumed from an
earlier checkpoint would fail every save when it reached step N again.
Before a lockfile save, process 0 now deletes any `*.__lock` files left
in the checkpoint directory while the other processes wait at a barrier.
This is safe because every process has finished its previous save and
none has opened the new save's stores yet, so each lock file present
belongs to a commit that can no longer finish. Removing it leaves the
store as OS locking would see it: the last committed manifest plus
unreferenced data files.

The tests check behavior rather than the requested mode: a commit under
the context a multi-process save uses waits for another writer's lock
file (it fails if the context ignores the locking setting), and a
two-process save into a directory holding an abandoned lock commits and
restores the new values (it times out if the cleanup is removed).

All runs below train the tiny June model on two Vultr MI355X nodes (EP8
within a node, data parallel across nodes) and save to the same NFS
directory.

| Setup | Before (OS locks) | After (lock files) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Save every 2 s | 7th of 7 saves failed | 80 of 80 committed | no
failures |
| Save every 30 s | not run | 26 of 26 committed, ~1 s per commit, 0.28
s median blocking per save | no failures |
| Kill and resume, `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` | blocked by
failed saves | every logged metric matches an uninterrupted run at every
step | resume is exact |

With saves requested every 2 s, lock files lengthen each commit from
about 3 s to about 10 s on this NFS, so back-to-back saves queue. At a
30 s interval the step time matched runs without frequent saves. With
the full 67B June model (weights plus MuonH state), all 10 saves of 503
GiB across two runs committed under lock files, each in 8.5 to 10.5 min,
about 1 GB/s to this NFS; the time is bandwidth-bound and step time is
unchanged while a save writes in the background.

A TensorStore OCDBT coordinator
(`ts.ocdbt.DistributedCoordinatorServer`) was also tried; on this NFS
every coordinated save failed.

A query with a prefix or wildcard-free `LIKE` on a string column of a
managed table fails at planning with `Invalid comparison operation:
Utf8View <= Utf8`. Examples are `key LIKE '/job/%'` on `log` and
`"cluster" LIKE 'cw-%'` on `iris.task_state`. The failure appeared on
the hub after #11184 was deployed.

Since #11184, planning hands every pushed-down filter to DataFusion's
`PruningPredicate`. DataFusion 53.1 rewrites such a `LIKE` into
comparisons of the column's min/max against `Utf8` literals, and the
provider types string columns as `Utf8View`, so the predicate fails to
evaluate.

Planning now builds the pruning predicate only from conjuncts that read
Int64 columns alone, the only columns with integer bounds. String
filters still prune through the key-range and trigram checks, and a time
filter beside a `LIKE` still prunes by `catalog_bounds`. A conjunct that
mixes a string column with an integer one, such as `key LIKE 'a%' OR
epoch_ms > N`, no longer prunes by the integer bounds.

A regression test reproduced the error before the change. The fix has
not run against production data.

[rl] Evaluate Snowball checkpoints on Harbor benchmarks (#10746)

The Snowball long loop can evaluate the starting policy and each scheduled checkpoint on fixed agentic benchmarks for tool calling, repository repair and terminal work, alongside EvalLite.

The `train-long-harbor` preset runs `train-long` with pinned BFCL, SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite cohorts from `rl_harbor.yaml`. Harbor runs the trials in Daytona sandboxes in the evaluation account selected by `DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY` and `DAYTONA_TARGET`, which submission requires, and builds each task environment inside its sandbox. The agents call the training run's inference server through its HTTP endpoint, which the preset turns on. Each agent's context limit is the engine's serving window, which covers prompt and reply tokens, and launch configuration refuses a reply cap that does not fit inside it. [Harbor evaluation recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/aab6f8d35b5f51fa7b2ca1591bd3b10815271979/docs/recipes/rl-experiments.md#harbor-evaluation)

The starting policy or a checkpoint is eligible for selection when at least 99% of the EvalLite active set and 90% of each Harbor cohort have a score. The Harbor callback adds Harbor rewards to the pooled `eval/all` average over every scored task, and best-checkpoint selection writes the eligible step with the highest pooled average to `best_checkpoint.json`. Per-cohort metrics are under `eval/harbor/<cohort>/`, `eval/harbor/wall_seconds` measures the whole Harbor evaluation, and trial artifacts are saved under `exports/inline_harbor/`. When Iris telemetry is available, each Harbor job sends its telemetry under the training run's ID.

Harbor retries a failed attempt whose sandbox teardown is unconfirmed, including after verification. This rule applies to offline Harbor evaluation, the Harbor review runtime and opt-in installed-agent training. FineStore archives require confirmed teardown for each selected attempt. The `2026.11.20.6` preset retries a trial once on each infrastructure error listed in `rl_harbor.yaml`, including `TmuxExecTimeoutError`, `DaytonaOutputUnavailable` and `MachineTerminated`. Concurrent Harbor jobs in one process share one telemetry exporter, which shuts down after the last job finishes.

commits.message:
[harbor] Complete trials whose session cleanup fails after a confirmed stop (#11464)

A trial whose agent-session cleanup fails now still records `completion`
when the environment stop that follows succeeds. The attempt keeps its
primary error and the cleanup error, so it is archived as a failed
attempt and the FineStore archive can seal.

Before this change, any non-cancellation error from either teardown step
set `_environment_cleanup_failed`. `_finalize` then skipped
`completion`, and the archive rejected the attempt as incomplete.
Stopping the environment ends every agent command.
`_stop_agent_environment` already sets the flag itself when the stop
fails, times out, or is cancelled. Teardown that is not confirmed still
leaves `completion` unset, and resume still retries those attempts.

In a 1600-trial TMax pilot, 5 attempts failed this way and the job ended
failed at finalize, although every result had been written. Each of the
5 recorded "Could not confirm agent session cleanup" after a successful
sandbox stop. Their primary errors were PhaseCancellationError (2),
DaytonaError (2) and TmuxCommandError (1).

[rl] Keep the assistant prefix's trailing whitespace in the prompt (#11654)

Render an unfinished assistant message with its trailing whitespace. The
chat template trims assistant content, and Hugging Face's
`continue_final_message` handling then right-strips the text before its
continuation tag, so a prefix that ends in a newline reached the model
without it. The closure grader joins the stored prefix, newline
included, with the reply, so such a reply was graded against a prefix
the model had not seen. The restored text is tokenized as a whole,
because the newline can merge with the preceding characters into one
token: with Grug's tokenizer a tool call's JSON ends in `}}` (3500) on
main and in `}}\n` (11498) here.

Since #11062 every closure row trains under this harness. On
`Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21`, the checkpoint
`train_quick_loop.py` starts snowball-100k from, I sampled rows of the
three closure strata whose prefix ends in a newline under both prompts,
on CPU from the public weights (temperature 1.0, one reply per prompt,
at most 512 new tokens). The prompt files and the decision rule were
fixed before sampling.

| stratum | rows | full credit, main's prompt | full credit, this prompt
| difference, points (95% interval) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `tool/tool_delimiter/close_required` | 100 | 0% | 75% | +75 (66 to 83)
|
| `code_fence/code_fence/close_required` | 200 | 6.5% | 16.5% | +10 (4
to 16) |
| `tool/repeated_opener_retention/opener_retention` | 100 | 58% | 40% |
-18 (-31 to -6) |

On the tool-call rows main's prompt ends at the JSON's closing brace,
and 94 of 100 replies are empty: the model emits a stop token at once
(146 of 200 on the code-fence rows). With the newline, 74 of 100
tool-call replies are `</tool_call>`. On the opener-retention rows

itself, and the grader accepts the doubled newline. With this tokenizer

commits.message:
[rl] Enforce groups per family and reuse committed checkpoints (#11711)

Train on fixed numbers of prompt groups by task family, select committed checkpoints during evaluation, and keep earlier agent turns when requests extend the same conversation.

`trainer.rollout_buffer.groups_per_family` sets the number of prompt groups from each family in every `full_batch` update. Fresh prompts follow a seeded order per family, and the checkpoint stores each order’s position. With fixed counts, each training row needs a named family, the counts must sum to `trainer.train_batch_size`, and `data.sampling.kind` must be unset. The launcher checks each Parquet pool, and the trainer checks it again after prompt-length filtering. Quarantine leaves enough distinct prompts in each family for all open batches. Recipes may omit the family map or supply positive counts.

When evaluation selects a new best at a nonzero step, checkpoint selection waits for any scheduled upload and uses the committed checkpoint for that step. After the trainer restores the latest checkpoint from the same run, evaluation can select it as a new best. An imported checkpoint selected by evaluation is saved into the receiving run's directory.

`AgentHarness` and `HarborTrialHarness` keep training turns together when a request without fixed prompt tokens extends an equivalent history after a normally completed turn. Equivalent histories can differ in tool argument JSON formatting or empty message fields. A compatible continuation can change the output cap. The model client uses the smallest of the request cap, sampling cap and available context. Pi treats a stop at the engine's turn limit or attempt token budget as a completed trial so Harbor can grade it. Pi also accepts an HTTP idle timeout in seconds for long waits between model responses.

The CatCount CPU canary ran with four groups per family before and after checkpoint recovery.

[levanter] Shard Snowball RNG at initialization (#11720)

Snowball weight initialization previously sampled full replicated arrays and resharded them afterward. Reuse the shared sharded `_init_weight` helper from `levanter.grug._moe.common` across Snowball initialization so each device generates only its own weight shard.

Move empty-mesh and absent-axis sharding resolution into `_current_sharding` in `levanter.grug.sharding`, use it in both `_init_weight` and Snowball checkpoint loading, and remove `_reshard_for_init`.

On an eight-device CPU mesh with partitionable Threefry enabled, Snowball initialization produces bit-identical weights and identical final shardings to the prior sample-then-reshard path while reducing compiler temporary allocation from 4,268,484 to 531,844 bytes.

commits.message:
[skyrl] Keep MuonH expert banks separate across model chunks (#11519)

Qualify each MuonH routed-expert bank id with its model chunk index.
With virtual pipeline stages, one rank holds several model chunks that
reuse local layer names, such as
`decoder.layers.0.mlp.experts.linear_fc2`. Under `expert_normalization:
all_experts`, `MegatronGrugMuonH.step` groups bank members by `(bank_id,
part_index)`, so these chunks' layers would merge into one bank and
share one Frobenius norm, with no error.

Nothing running today is affected. The Grug Megatron bridge raises on
virtual pipeline parallelism, so every Grug run has one chunk per rank.
`all_experts` is opt-in, and the default is `per_expert`, which passes
no banks. This fix is for when either restriction is lifted.

A single chunk gives the same results as before. Bank ids gain the same
`0.` prefix, so grouping, the `sorted` order of bank updates and the
order of expert-parallel norm all-reduces stay the same. Bank ids are
kept outside optimizer state and checkpoints. The new CPU test steps two
chunks with identical local names and differently scaled weights
together, then compares them exactly with independent per-chunk
optimizers. It fails without the prefix (12 of 12 elements differ, max
0.146).

commits.message:
[levanter] Select grug QB thresholds by radix select on AMD Instinct (#11144)

Select each expert's per-shard QB threshold with an exact Pallas-Triton
radix select (`levanter.kernels.pallas.radix_select`) on AMD Instinct

µs). The result equals `top_k` bit for bit, except that at a tie between
-0.0 and +0.0 either zero may come back.

checks).

LiveCodeBench collects competitive-programming problems from LeetCode,
AtCoder and Codeforces as their contests are released. The model writes
one Python program per problem, and the program passes when it passes
every public and private test.

Data comes from
[`livecodebench/code_generation_lite`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/livecodebench/code_generation_lite/tree/0fe84c3912ea0c4d4a78037083943e8f0c4dd505)

[eval] Let curated runs save a task reference instead of the TaskSpec (#11661)

Add `--task-evidence {embedded,reference}` to the evaluation launcher.
Curated attempt evidence (`evaluation/attempts/<sha>.json`) has embedded
a full copy of the TaskSpec, hidden test resources included, in every
attempt. With `reference`, an attempt keeps only its item's task id and
source row; the run record's corpus manifest, whose dataset id pins
every shard's sha256, already identifies the task. `embedded` stays the
default and is omitted from serialized settings, and like request
concurrency the setting is left out of run identity, so existing run ids
are unchanged and an interrupted run resumes under either mode. Nothing
reads the embedded copy: retries use the saved conversations and grade.

The copies are what broke the full LiveCodeBench (#11396) run on TPU.
The v5e serving hosts are in us-west4 and the records bucket is in
us-central1, and the run's evidence exceeded the 10 GB cross-region
budget. On a branch combining this change with #11396, qwen3-8b on a
v5litepod-4 with `--task-evidence reference` graded all 1,055 problems
with 560 MB of results and scored 72.1%, against 72.6% for the earlier
embedded run on an H100. Results for the 20-problem smoke run fell from
28.2 MB to 3.9 MB.

Letting a benchmark declare `reference` as its own default is left for
when LiveCodeBench and LiveCodeBench Pro, whose hidden tests are 15 GB,

commits.message:
[finelog] Prune segments by catalog min/max of flagged columns (#11184)

A one-hour search of Finelog's `log` opens almost every file in the
table: an `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of one such query had about 1,660 candidate
files. `log` is keyed by `key`, so key bounds can't prune by time. But
each file covers a short time span (median 0.5 h), and #11394 stores
each segment's `epoch_ms` min/max in the catalog. With this PR, planning
drops a segment whose range misses a filter on a `catalog_bounds` column
before it opens the file.

Planning hands each segment's integer bounds (an Int64 key, `seq`, and
the `catalog_bounds` columns) to DataFusion's `PruningPredicate`, so the
`epoch_ms > extract(epoch from now()) * 1000 - …` form, `IN` lists and
`OR`s prune as well. A segment without bounds for a filtered column, or
one recorded as always-scan, reports null and is kept, so missing bounds
never change a result. String key bounds and partitions keep their own
checks, and a legacy-local table is always scanned. `lib/finelog/OPS.md`
now writes its time bounds as integer comparisons and explains when they
prune.

Queries with and without column bounds returned the same rows for five
time filters, whether no segment, some segments or every segment had
bounds, and after the backfill. The physical scan opened the expected
number of segment files for each.

This PR adds no stored state; it only reads what #11394 writes. Pruning
applies to segments that already have bounds, and older segments gain
them as #11394's backfill progresses. Rolling back to an image without
this PR returns to scanning every segment, with the same results.

Terminus-2's tmux liveness, capture and kill commands are now bounded at

bounded tmux exec, including the batched call, goes through one helper

[finelog] Keep function names in the server binary (#11754)

The Finelog release profile no longer strips the symbol table, so `perf`
and gdb report function names for a deployed server. The deploy image
removes the debug info with `strip --strip-debug` after the build. The
wheel profile still strips everything.

A CPU profile of the stripped hub binary prints raw addresses. Mapping
them to functions by hand put the hot function about 0x1000 away from
the true one and led to #11279, a fix for code that was not hot. Keeping
the names in the binary was chosen over publishing a symbol file per
build because it needs no storage, no lookup by build identity, and no
extra step at profiling time.

`strip = "debuginfo"` in the profile would be the one-line way to keep
names and drop debug info. It does not work in the image. mold 1.10.1,
the linker the image installs from Debian bookworm, drops the symbol
table on `--strip-debug`: a build with that setting had no `.symtab`,
and a hello-world crate reproduces it with mold and not with the default
linker. The profile therefore keeps everything and binutils `strip`
removes the debug info.

Sizes of `finelog-server` for linux/amd64, built with rustc 1.100.0 in
`rust:1-bookworm`:

| Build | Symbols | Size | gzip -6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `strip = "symbols"` (before) | 0 | 138.2 MB | 47.3 MB |
| `strip = "none"` | 406,914 | 209.6 MB | 58.5 MB |
| `strip = "none"`, then `strip --strip-debug` (this change) | 406,914 |
185.6 MB | 52.8 MB |

The image grows by 47.4 MB uncompressed, about 5.5 MB compressed.
`finelog-migrate` is 27.8 MB with 68,809 symbols; its size before was
not measured.

Removing the symbol table does not change what the server runs. Running
`strip --strip-debug` or `strip --strip-all` on the `strip = "none"`
binary leaves all 34 loaded sections byte-identical. The only differing
bytes in the loadable segments are six in the ELF header that locate the
section table.

Changing the Cargo setting changes the code layout once, as any commit
to the crate does. Cargo hashes the profile into each crate's metadata
(`cfg_if` gets a different `-C metadata` under each strip setting),
which changes mangled names and the order functions are laid out in. The
`symbols` and `none` builds of one commit have the same code size to
within 0.01% (140,312,339 and 140,303,827 loaded bytes) but only 8 of 34
loaded sections are byte-identical. Two builds with the same setting
differ only in the build timestamp and the build ID. The run-time effect
of the different layout was not measured; the builds ran under amd64
emulation, which is not a usable benchmark host. Compare the hub's CPU
use before and after the first deploy that includes this change.

Frame pointers are unchanged.

[grug] Stop parameter drift at learning rate zero (#11755)

A 15-update Snowball SFT run at learning rate 0 still changed 8.16% of
one expert bank by one BF16 code step. The scale-invariant
re-projections in the MuonH hyperball and AdamH transforms computed the
parameter-space norm in the parameter dtype while the post-step norm
stayed float32, so the re-projection rescaled every step by the rounding
error of that norm. At learning rate 0 this left a one-BF16-step update
on part of every matrix group; at positive rates it biased the Frobenius
re-projection at every step.

Compute the step, both norms, and the re-projection from float32
upcasts, and rescale by the ratio of the two norms. Equal norms give a
ratio of exactly 1.0, so a zero raw step produces an exactly zero update
without a special case. The update is cast back to the parameter dtype.

Measured Frobenius-norm drift of the scale-invariant groups over 15
steps at learning rate 0.01 (MuonH config, tiny MoE tree, per-step mean
and total over steps):

| BF16 leaf | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| attention w_q | +1.5e-4/step, total +2.2e-3 | +9.4e-6/step, total
+1.4e-4 |
| shared expert w_gate | +3.2e-4/step, total +4.8e-3 | -1.3e-5/step,
total -1.9e-4 |
| expert bank w_gate | +1.4e-5/step, max single step 4.7e-3 |
-1.6e-6/step, total -2.5e-5 |
| output projection | +8.3e-5/step, total +1.2e-3 | +9.9e-6/step, total
+1.5e-4 |

The sign of the bias depends on how each leaf's BF16 norm rounding
lands; the defect is the per-step bias itself. After the change the BF16
residual is storage rounding of the stored update, and FP32 storage
stays at 1-ulp noise (about 1e-8 per step before and after).

Zero-rate bit-identity now holds for `grug_moe_muonh_v1` and
`grug_moe_adamh_v2` under BF16 and FP32 parameter policies, and the BF16
norm-preservation test at a positive rate fails on the old code.

[harbor] Classify three Daytona sandbox failures as retryable (#11675)

Classify three Daytona sandbox failures as retryable infrastructure in
Harbor's error taxonomy: connection resets (`DaytonaConnectionError`),
tmux execs that outlive their deadline (`TmuxExecTimeoutError`), and
command output that cannot be read back from the sandbox
(`DaytonaOutputUnavailable`). Marin's Harbor runner treats any error
name missing from the taxonomy as unknown, so one such trial marked a
whole run infra-failed with no metrics.

Two of these had no specific name. When a sandbox stopped responding,
terminus-2's batched tmux call surfaced as a bare `TimeoutError`; it now
raises `TmuxExecTimeoutError`. Model commands run inside tmux, so only
an unresponsive sandbox holds that exec open past its requested waits
plus the 180-second margin. Shellbox's Daytona backend raised
`RuntimeError("Cannot collect Daytona command output")` when stdout or
stderr could not be downloaded before the output-collection deadline; it
now raises `DaytonaOutputUnavailable`, a `RuntimeError` subclass.

All three hit full 300-task SWE-bench Multilingual runs of Qwen3.5 and
Qwen3.6 (#11676): 9–10 connection resets and 5–7 tmux timeouts per run,
plus one lost command output during terminus-2 setup on

commits.author: penfever
commits.message:
[levanter] Add opt-in bounded lookahead window to the SFT packer (#11379)

Opt-in bounded first-fit lookahead for `pack_documents`, configured with
`DatasetComponent.pack_lookahead_window`. The default (`None`) keeps the
sequential packer byte-for-byte.

The sequential packer closes a sequence whenever the next in-order
document does not fit. On Experiment 2's 216 pinned SFT caches at
262,144 positions with a 64-segment cap, 13.9% of packed sequences
(143,933 of 1,035,158) close while they still had room for the next
document, and 13.63% of positions are padding. With a lookahead window
set, a pack that cannot take its frontier document takes the first
fitting document among up to `lookahead_window` documents starting at
that one (window 1 is equivalent to the sequential packer). Skipped
documents stay pending and keep their relative order, so reordering
stays local; with a lookahead, packs can hold non-contiguous documents.
The reader computes per-document token spans and applies
`slice_strategy` in one helper for both pack representations. Setting
the window on an unpacked component raises instead of being silently
ignored.

Measured on the Experiment 2 population (216 chat caches, offsets only,
capacity 262,144, cap 64):

| Packer | Packed sequences | Padding |
|---|---:|---:|
| sequential (baseline) | 1,035,158 | 13.6267% |
| lookahead window 8 | 979,589 | 8.7270% |
| lookahead window 64 | 970,215 | 7.8451% |

The remaining floor is the 64-segment cap, not document order: with the
cap, the lower bound is 7.00% padding, and 99.9% of that bound's padding
comes from the 39 sources whose conversations are short enough that 64
of them cannot reach 262,144 tokens. The lookahead implementation
produces exactly the same packs as the offline simulation on five real
caches, including the largest (3.6M documents) and segment-cap-bound
caches. Full tables, per-source breakdowns, reorder distances, and
packer costs: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11380.

Part of #11380

commits.author: atqamar
commits.message:
[rl] Run Snowball experiments from presets and publish results (#10740)

To compare changes to Snowball’s inference engine, trainer or training
data, run experiments from named presets with recorded inputs and saved
results.

`rl.py` holds no model settings: each model file (here `snowball_rl.py`)
declares its presets, controls and model name, and calls the shared
runner, which handles planning, submission, waiting and status. The
model name labels the W&B run, the finelog records, the Marina row and
each evaluation row, so two models' runs stay separate in every sink.
Snowball's presets form two groups. The short loop (also called the
quick loop) compares one change against control runs: generation speed,
training speed, learning and data screening. The long loop trains a
model and keeps its best checkpoint: `train-long` evaluates the 100-task
EvalLite active set at step 0 and every ten updates, records the best
eligible step and exports that step to Hugging Face format. Every
Snowball preset restricts NCCL to the InfiniBand rails
(`NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp`).

`--plan` composes each launch on CPU and runs the training driver's own
configuration checks, so a setting the driver would refuse, such as a
batch smaller than the data-parallel size or an unknown Harbor task
setting, fails before any GPU is requested. Before a gated submission,
the launcher composes the candidate on CPU and checks that the saved
control runs named by the preset's control pin match the current preset
configuration. After the runs finish, the comparison requires matching
evaluation requests and held-out task content, then saves the
measurements and a verdict with its reasons. The checked-in pins are for
`2026.11.06.1`. Until pins for the current preset revision,
`2026.11.20.3`, are checked in, gated launches and control publication
stop and print the command that collects them.

At the end of `--run --wait`, the launcher publishes available terminal
attempts for `learning-medium`, `data-medium` and `train-long` using the
caller's Marina login. The `publish` command also sends a selected
stored attempt or the pinned learning controls. Marina groups records by
run and lets readers pick an attempt to see its evaluation scores,
available verdict and failed checks. Records can link to the W&B run,
Grafana window, experiment issue and EvalDash runs. A GitHub experiment
issue is optional: `--issue N` links the run to it, and the run-rl skill
asks the experimenter whether to open a new issue, use an existing one
or not track the run, then posts one comment per result with a fixed set
of fields after the experimenter approves it.

The `compare` command recomputes a candidate's verdict from saved
outputs on CPU. The EvalLite scorer reports coverage for a chosen
version and computes its score when every active task has verified
answers with the matching task ID and content digest. [RL experiment
recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/82a60d0c42c2d04aee8e2913ef1cd1792c291a81/docs/recipes/rl-experiments.md)

[rl] Record SkyRL attempts and run named evaluations (#10737)

To trace a SkyRL result across launches and checkpoint resumes, save
attempt records, training metrics and per-task evaluation scores
alongside the run’s artifacts.

The `records` backend writes numeric metrics by attempt and step. Each
attempt’s receipt pairs the composed configuration with the job’s status
and recorded start and finish times. Jobs that use the `records` backend
run without Iris retries. After a preemption, a new attempt resumes from
the saved checkpoint with a fresh attempt ID. The metrics reader
includes parent metrics through the checkpoint step and keeps the newest
value and its attempt ID when metrics overlap. Evaluation records retain
each task’s answer scores and verification outcomes.

Named evaluations can use separate datasets, sampling settings and
answer counts. Each named evaluation can run at every evaluation point
or only at the final training update. Evaluation-only jobs with local
engines allocate inference GPUs. The launcher checks training settings,
distributed layout and evaluation schedules on CPU before submission.

`finestore.rl.run_records.read_evaluations` and `read_attempt_metrics`
read these records, so checkpoint scores can be compared and each score
traced to its evaluation settings and per-task verification results.

commits.message:
[datakit] Require core and Uncheatable evals in the decontam corpus (#10541)

Eval corpus preparation now stops before it seals a manifest when a
required eval fails to load. The required evals are the nine AA
Intelligence Index benchmarks, a new Uncheatable Eval suite (the seven
subsets that `experiments/datasets/uncheatable.py` evaluates, pinned to
upstream commit 185c4638 with exact record counts), and every lm-eval
task that is not in `BEST_EFFORT_LMH_TASKS`. That table maps each of 116
tasks to the reason that it does not load; the other 223 tasks are
required, among them gsm8k, humaneval, mmlu, mmlu_pro and
leaderboard_mmlu_pro. A new eval must load, or be added to the table on
purpose. Each of the 20 group tasks also has a pinned number of leaf
tasks (`LMH_LEAF_TASK_COUNTS`, for example 57 for mmlu), and a task that
is not pinned must load as one leaf, so a group that loads only some of
its subtasks fails. The eval Bloom build takes a tuple of
`RequiredEvalSuite`s and refuses to start unless the AA and Uncheatable
manifests are complete and the lm-eval manifest lists every required
task with its pinned number of leaf tasks and at least one record in
each.

GSM8K failed in every region because the Hub no longer resolves the
un-namespaced `gsm8k` ID, and MMLU failed on CoreWeave after a dropped
connection. Preparation logged and skipped both, so the Hero's decontam
marks (`_combined_fixed_8c17764d` Bloom, built from the CoreWeave
corpus) never checked MMLU or GSM8K. Uncheatable Eval was never in the
corpus, although the Hero evaluates it in its training loop.

The loader patch maps `gsm8k` to `openai/gsm8k`. Required lm-eval task
loads retry five times with exponential backoff, and source downloads
use the shared retrying HTTP session, so a dropped connection no longer
stops preparation. A sealed corpus version is immutable, so

staged and sealed in `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`,

`gs://marin-us-central2`, the four prefixes that held v4, so the Datakit
canaries can build the Bloom after merge. Each regional lm-eval manifest

tasks. The 116 best-effort tasks still fail; #11503 tracks them.

commits.author: chrismc91
commits.message:
[eval] Add SuperGPQA with a hashed sample order (#11688)

Add [SuperGPQA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/m-a-p/SuperGPQA)
([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14739)) as the curated chat
benchmark `supergpqa`: 26,529 graduate-level multiple-choice questions
across 13 disciplines, each with 4 to 10 options, pinned at dataset
commit `4430d445` (ODC-By). The prompt, greedy decoding and letter
extraction are ported from the authors' zero-shot runner at
[`e31e8bf`](https://github.com/SuperGPQA/SuperGPQA/tree/e31e8bf3e7089aef808be5ddecafd4538dee6e41);
grading is programmatic, with no judge. The extraction is a new option
on verifyit's MCQ mode, `McqSpec(extraction=SUPERGPQA_REFERENCE,
option_texts=...)`, implemented in `verifyit/supergpqa_extraction.py`.
The grader reads only the final answer
(`response_selection="final_only"`), as the runner does for API
reasoning models, so an answer cut off mid-reasoning scores as a miss.
Scores are also reported per discipline and per difficulty.
`supergpqa-sample` in `configs/evalchemy.yaml` selects 2,500 rows for
routine runs. Neither is added to a suite.

The full set costs about $130 to $160 per 30B-class model on H100s, so
routine runs use a sample. SuperGPQA's protocol selects rows with
`CohortOrder.SHUFFLED` from #11765, so `--limit N` takes a fixed uniform
sample; SuperGPQA's file is grouped unevenly, and its first 500 rows
differ from the population by up to 22 points in discipline share. This
PR is stacked on #11765.

The port matches the reference. All 26,529 compiled prompts are
byte-identical to the runner's rendering. On 185,703 synthetic responses
(seven styles per row), the new MCQ mode and the runner's extractor
agree on every extracted letter, and rescoring all 7,000 stored
responses with it reproduces every score below. The runner's regexes
backtrack exponentially on short runs of `*`, `(` or `\`; about 24
characters take seconds. The runner bounds each search with a 5-second
timeout and counts a timeout as no match. The port keeps that timeout
with `SIGALRM` and restores any timer the caller had set. Because
`SIGALRM` works only on the main thread, the mode refuses to run
elsewhere, and SuperGPQA tasks grade in a grader machine instead of
in-process.

Sample runs, all on `cw-us-east-02a`:

[eval] Request 12 GB instead of 32 GB for curated eval graders (#11662)

Lower the curated-eval grading job's request from 8 CPUs and 32 GB to 8
CPUs and 12 GB. No CPU-only VM in the `marin` cluster has 32 GB
(`cpu_vm_e2_highmem_2_ondemand` VMs have 16 GB), so graders could only
use memory left over on TPU hosts. On a busy cluster a LiveCodeBench
smoke grader waited more than an hour for a 32 GB slot while its TPU
inference server sat idle; with 12 GB the same job was placed within 20
seconds.

Iris records a task's peak memory from `docker stats` on its container
every 5 seconds, which includes the grader's bubblewrap sandboxes.
Across 106 curated-eval graders from 13 to 17 November (a few hours of
telemetry timed out and are missing), the largest peak was 7.6 GiB (full
LiveCodeBench, 1,055 problems), and two full LongBench v2 runs peaked at
7.2 and 6.6 GiB; most graders peaked at 1.2 to 2 GiB. A full
LiveCodeBench run with the 12 GB request peaked at 5.5 GiB. The request
is also the container's memory limit, so a heavier benchmark would be
killed rather than slowed; one that needs more should declare its own
grading resources then.

commits.author: karansag
commits.message:
[eval] Prepare candidate and hosted judge weights before serving either (#11694)

An evaluation batch with a hosted judge now prepares the candidate and
judge
checkpoints in parallel and waits for both before it submits any serving
job.
Before, the batch opened the candidate session (prepare, then
accelerator
serve) and only then prepared the judge, so a cold judge's CPU download
held
the warm candidate's GPUs idle.

remote_inference is now prepare_inference, which pins Hugging Face
revisions
and, where the placement allows, fills the serving cache from CPU jobs,
followed by
serve_inference, which takes the returned PreparedInference.
Single-model
callers keep remote_inference, which runs the two steps in order. Each
role
keeps its own serving config and placement. A failed preparation of
either
role records an infrastructure failure under that role's name and
submits no
accelerator job. Serving readiness retries no longer re-enter
preparation.

Policy-finalization runs serve their answer-equivalence judge from
inside each
policy-judged evaluation. The batch now lists that judge in
prepared_judges, so
its weights are prepared alongside the candidate, and the evaluation's
own
prepare is a cache check. The batch does not serve it.

Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11173

[taskcompendium] Add a hashed cohort order for uniform --limit samples (#11765)

Add `CohortOrder.SHUFFLED`, a cohort order that sorts candidate rows by
a SHA-256 hash of their source row. With it, `--limit N` selects a fixed
uniform sample, and a larger limit extends a smaller one. A protocol
opts in with `cohort=CohortPolicy(order=CohortOrder.SHUFFLED)`. It
cannot be combined with task groups; that combination raises.

`--limit` otherwise takes the first N rows in file order. Some datasets
are grouped unevenly: in SuperGPQA, the first 500 rows differ from the
population by up to 22 points in discipline share. Under `SHUFFLED`,
SuperGPQA's 20-item smoke run drew rows 4 through 26,398, and its
2,500-row sample matched the population within 1.3 points on discipline,
difficulty and calculation share.

No existing benchmark switches. The default order stays `SOURCE`, so
earlier `--limit` results remain comparable. A benchmark that adopts
`SHUFFLED` gets a new protocol fingerprint, so its limited runs are not
mixed with earlier first-N runs. Selection records now carry a rank for
any non-source order.

Split from #11688, which uses this order for SuperGPQA.

commits.message:
[verifyit] Grade on Python 3.10 grader machines (#11738)

The staged verifyit runtime imports on the grader machine's own
interpreter
from copied package directories, and the declared grader environments
include Python 3.10 workspace images. Attempts on those machines stopped
at
`from enum import StrEnum` and returned an infrastructure error instead
of
a verdict; lowering the floor alone would have stopped them on the
tomllib
fallback, because staging installs no dependency metadata.

Lower the package floor to Python 3.10 and make the staged runtime
self-contained. verifyit gains a compat module with a version-gated
StrEnum
backport and a tomli fallback for tomllib, judge retry timing uses
timezone.utc where datetime.UTC is 3.11-only, and tomli ships as a
dependency for interpreters below 3.11. The task runtime stages the
tomli
and tomli_w package directories beside verifyit, so the grader imports
the
same modules a pip install would provide.

New tests stage the package directories into uv-managed 3.10 and 3.11
venvs the way the runtime build does, sweep every verifyit module
import,
and grade a numeric case through the verifyit entry.

Fixes #11721

[eval] Add FACTS Grounding v2 graded by a single gpt-oss-120b judge (#11753)

Add `facts-grounding-v2`, the public half of [FACTS
Grounding](https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/google/facts-grounding/leaderboard)
v2 ([arXiv:2512.10791](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10791), section 6).
Each item gives the model a document of up to about 38k tokens and a
request about it; a response scores 1 when it addresses the request and
every factual sentence is supported by the document. The rows are the
856 examples in Kaggle dataset `deepmind/FACTS-grounding-examples`
version 17 (CC-BY-4.0), pinned by URL and SHA-256. The Hugging Face
mirror `google/FACTS-grounding-public` is the 860-row v1 release; Google
later dropped four of its rows. The model receives each row's
`full_prompt` as one user message with thinking enabled and a
16,384-token cap, and the judge sees only the final answer.

Grading follows the v2 [starter
notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/prathameshbang/facts-grounding-v2-benchmark-starter)
(version 4), with its prompts copied byte for byte and its verdict
parsers ported line for line. The judge writes its own answer to the
prompt, rates the response's instruction following against it, and, for
an eligible response, labels every sentence as supported, not supported,
or making no claim. The notebook asks Gemini 2.5 Flash and then GPT-5
and averages their grounding verdicts; this eval asks the run's
configured judge, `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together, for every step.
Scores are therefore not comparable to the Kaggle leaderboard, which
also includes an 859-row private split. Other deliberate differences: a
judge transport failure is retried and then reported as an
infrastructure error instead of being scored, CRLF line breaks in judge
replies are normalized before parsing, and judge replies may use 32,768
tokens. The scorer calls the judge through a new `verifyit` helper,
`judge_reply`, which reuses the existing transport retries.

| Model | Run | Scored | Factuality ± SE | Eligible | Truncated |
Reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | full | 855/856 | 0.740 ± 0.015 | 0.973 | 0 |
0.721 (95% CI 0.697–0.743), V2 judges, NeMo Gym
[#3661](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/pull/3661) |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | full | 855/856 | 0.795 ± 0.014 | 0.930 | 0 | none
published |
| Snowball v0.1 | full | 856/856 | 0.487 ± 0.017 | 0.952 | 0 | none
published |

The Glimmer and Nemotron runs used the protocol before the CRLF and
judge-cap fixes; the Snowball run used the final protocol. Snowball was
served from the 09-25 campaign's model config with vLLM's `grug`
reasoning parser added, so its reasoning stays out of the graded answer;
one Snowball answer contains a stray `<|end_think|>` between two drafts
and was graded as written. Glimmer and Nemotron each lost one item whose
4,500 to 6,000-token answer exhausted the earlier 16,384-token judge
cap, and three items in total scored 0 because the judge separated its
sentence verdicts with CRLF. Nemotron's score sits within NeMo Gym's
interval, which was measured with the two v2 judges on the same 856
rows.

A blinded review checked the grader against contracts written from the
v2 prompt text. Two language-model reviewers (Claude Opus and Claude
Sonnet) labeled 42 frozen cases sampled by grader verdict from the
Glimmer and Nemotron full runs, with lean agreement 0.93 (kappa 0.63).
All 13 sampled passes were confirmed; every error was a false fail,
giving a stratum-weighted error rate of 19% (95% CI 15–23%) against
reviewer consensus. A non-blind check of the judge's flagged sentences
found two real errors the reviewers missed, so the true rate is likely
13–16%. Most false fails fall in two places. In 7 of 7 sampled
ineligible verdicts, both reviewers judged the response eligible;
`gpt-oss-120b` repeats its "Major Issue(s)" rating in 79% of re-runs, so
a second vote from the same model would rarely change it, and the v2
protocol's second judge from another model family is not reproduced
here. The judge ruled 7.0% of Glimmer's responses ineligible, 4.8% of
Snowball's and 2.7% of Nemotron's. The other false fails come from the
judge rejecting short inferences that the v2 prompt allows as "strongly
implied". The eligibility judge is an open question.

| Glimmer full | H100x2 | 23 min | 28 min | 0.94 | 5.79 |
| Nemotron full | H100x4 | 42 min | 52 min | 3.46 | 21.33 |
| Snowball full | H100x8 | 29 min | 34 min | 4.51 | 27.75 |

Each run also had one or two preempted inference attempts whose duration
